question: How can a chorus sound both overwhelming and afraid?
intro: Four orchestral blows open a choral vision of judgement. The violence later recedes towards the trembling of those who face it. This two-minute track contains only the opening Dies irae number, not the whole sequence or Requiem. Unlike Berlioz’s finale, Verdi sets the medieval words to his own music rather than quoting their familiar plainchant melody; compare that distinction in the Dies irae thread.

sections.label: The day of wrath
sections.mNote: Choral declamation and orchestral blows establish the threat

sections.label: The force recedes
sections.mNote: The opening rhetoric diminishes into more exposed phrases

sections.label: Trembling before judgement
sections.mNote: Repeated quiet syllables turn collective power into fear

cues.title: Four blows, then voices
cues.text: The opening score sets four separated orchestral blows against rushing figures, then brings in the chorus. Listen for the difference between the sharp attacks and the moving texture around them. The judgement scene gains force from interruption as well as sheer volume.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, PDF pages 21–22, opening of No. 2. Report: the first five-second window includes separated attacks, followed by a much stronger window at 0:05. Exact choral entry is not synchronised.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Words older than the music
cues.text: Dies irae means “day of wrath”. The medieval sequence describes judgement, terror and the plea for mercy. Verdi sets its words without using the familiar plainchant tune quoted by Berlioz: a shared text does not by itself establish a borrowed melody.
cues.evidence: The Latin text and Verdi’s independent setting are visible in the score; compare Berlioz’s labelled chant quotation. The Boston Philharmonic event description for 23 November 2025, paragraph beginning “Day of wrath”, identifies the medieval sequence: https://www.bso.org/events/bpo-verdi-2025 .

cues.title: For Alessandro Manzoni
cues.text: Manzoni’s death in May 1873 prompted Verdi to complete a Requiem in his honour. The first performance took place at San Marco in Milan on 22 May 1874, the anniversary of the writer’s death. A public memorial gave this private admiration a large musical form.
cues.evidence: David Rosen, critical-edition introduction, p. xvi, on Manzoni and the decision to complete the work; Teatro dell’Opera di Roma historical archive gives the Milan premiere date and venue.

cues.title: The force begins to recede
cues.text: The opening’s sustained force gives way to a quieter span. Listen for how exposed the words become when the orchestral weight diminishes. Fear need not sound like another explosion: the withdrawal changes the chorus’s relation to the threat it has described.
cues.evidence: Report: level falls from −9.5 dB at 1:00 to roughly −20 dB at 1:10–1:25; a structural change is detected at 1:06.

cues.title: An earlier memorial plan
cues.text: After Rossini died, Verdi proposed a Requiem shared among Italian composers and contributed a Libera me in 1869. That planned performance did not happen. He later revised his contribution for the Manzoni Requiem, giving the new work roots in an earlier act of commemoration.
cues.evidence: David Rosen, critical-edition introduction, pp. xi–xvi: the Messa per Rossini project, Verdi’s Libera me and the later decision to complete his own Requiem.

cues.title: A chorus made to tremble
cues.text: The closing part of this number sets “Quantus tremor” — how great the trembling — in restrained, repeated choral syllables. Listen to the collective voice becoming vulnerable. The score’s quiet articulation matters as much as the opening’s force.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, PDF pages 39–42, repeated choral notes at Quantus tremor. Report: the later region remains below the opening’s level and has frequent attacks around 1:35–1:50; placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An opening, not the whole sequence
cues.text: This track stops before Tuba mirum, the next part of the sequence. In the complete Requiem, the violent Dies irae music returns later; those returns are not present in this excerpt. Do not mistake this file’s ending for the work’s final response to judgement.
cues.evidence: The Commons track is part 03, opening Dies irae. Eulenburg score page 43 begins Tuba mirum; the complete score contains later returns of the opening Dies irae material.

transitions.title: Power gives way to exposure
transitions.how: The chorus and orchestra do not sustain the opening weight indefinitely. Repeated diminution and thinner accompaniment make the words more exposed. The same judgement scene is heard from a more vulnerable scale.
transitions.evidence: Score, diminishing passage on PDF pages 36–38; report boundary at 1:06 and approximately ten-decibel reduction between 1:00 and 1:10.

transitions.title: Declamation becomes trembling
transitions.how: The broad opening declamation yields to repeated, restrained syllables. The accompaniment remains active, but the chorus’s articulation makes fear audible through small reiterated gestures rather than another massed outburst.
transitions.evidence: Score, Quantus tremor on PDF pages 39–42. Report changes around 1:24–1:36 and increased attack density in the later restrained span; this is an approximate division, not text alignment.

source.title: Verdi, Requiem — Eulenburg full score, plate E.E.4864
source.locator: PDF pages 21–42, opening Dies irae number. “Tuba” represents the score’s ophicleide/bass-brass staff, not a verified instrument used in this transfer. No solo singers occur in this number; the offstage trumpets belong to the following Tuba mirum.

timeline.note: Four orchestral blows and rushing figures; the chorus enters after the opening attacks.
Choral entry region; lower and upper voices enter in succession, not as one instantaneous block.
Expanded opening declamation, including bass-drum punctuation in the written score.
Diminishing region with progressively reduced scoring; not every group sounds continuously.
Quiet Quantus tremor region: repeated choral notes, active strings and restrained wind support.

composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made a change of vocal phrase, bass note or ensemble balance alter the relations between people on stage.
facts: Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto; private study with Vincenzo Lavigna in Milan after rejection by the Conservatoire
La Scala, Milan · La Fenice, Venice · Paris Opéra · theatres in Naples, Rome, St Petersburg and Cairo
Francesco Maria Piave, Salvadore Cammarano and Arrigo Boito among his principal librettists
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred pieces, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Verdi was born in Le Roncole, near Busseto, where his parents kept an inn and shop. He learnt the organ locally and studied with Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto. The merchant and amateur musician Antonio Barezzi helped finance further training in Milan, but the Conservatoire rejected him in 1832. Private study with Vincenzo Lavigna, who had worked at La Scala, gave him access to counterpoint and practical theatrical knowledge instead. In 1836 he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took up municipal musical duties in Busseto. His route to opera passed through a provincial network of patronage, church work and teaching.

The first opera, Oberto, reached La Scala in 1839 and secured further commissions. By then Verdi had lost his daughter Virginia; his son Icilio died that year, and Margherita died in 1840. The comedy Un giorno di regno failed at La Scala in September 1840. Nabucco brought success in March 1842. Temistocle Solera’s libretto offered large public scenes, sharply opposed groups and an exiled people whose collective song could carry a dramatic burden usually assigned to a principal singer.
